learningObjective: Trace why keeping only each block's local top-k and merging it with the running top-k preserves the exact global top-k without storing the full query-by-item score matrix.
mediumRationale: A semantic table is the smallest medium that keeps block boundaries, local candidates, and the evolving retained set aligned in one worked trace. Readers can verify the top-2 invariant row by row, while the table remains text-native, screen-reader accessible, responsive, and printable without a client-side runtime.

mediumComparison.mermaid: Rejected because the lesson depends on comparing concrete ranked scores at each pass; a flowchart would show control flow but hide the selection invariant.
mediumComparison.svg: Rejected because fixed-coordinate matrix cells add authoring and mobile-label risk when a native table expresses the discrete trace more accessibly.
mediumComparison.semanticHtml: Selected because a compact table aligns each scored block with its local top-2 and running top-2, exposes the exact numeric merge, and reflows within the established responsive figure primitive.
mediumComparison.interaction: Rejected because stepping through blocks would hide states that are more useful when shown together and would add controls without changing the invariant.
mediumComparison.paperReuse: Rejected because the reviewed sources establish cosine scoring and partition semantics but do not provide this memory-bounded merge trace. No external figure, data, wording, or layout is reused.
mediumComparison.noVisual: Rejected because prose states the loop but leaves readers to mentally prove why discarded non-top-k items can never enter the final top-k and how the persistent candidate set stays bounded.

pages.insight: The preceding PCA slide ends with dimensionality reduction followed by K-nearest-neighbor clustering, providing embedding-space context but no retrieval execution detail.
The clustering slide lists cosine among similarity measures and discusses materializing similarity matrices, but does not address memory-bounded scoring or incremental top-k selection.

The K-nearest-neighbor slide describes comparing a query with every stored example and uses a full distance vector followed by argsort; it motivates exact retrieval but materializes and sorts all scores rather than blocking and merging candidates.
The following random-forest slide marks the end of the nearest-neighbor neighborhood and adds no retrieval or selection mechanism.

sources.title: Introduction to Information Retrieval: Dot products
sources.usage: Used as an authoritative textbook source to verify that cosine similarity is the dot product of length-normalized vectors and that retrieval chooses the items with the highest resulting similarities.
sources.license: The online Cambridge University Press textbook is used only for mathematical semantics. No permissive artwork reuse grant was established, so no figure, example data, prose, or layout is copied.

sourceReview.notes: The hardest prose-only mental model is the exactness invariant. After a block is scored, any item outside that block's local top-k has at least k items in the same block scoring no lower, so it cannot belong to the global top-k. Therefore the only candidates needed after each pass are the previous running top-k and the new block's local top-k. The original example follows one query with k = 2 across three blocks and makes persistent O(k) state distinct from transient block scores.

agentReview.summary: Read the complete article, indexed all 214 deck pages and inspected the full nearest-neighbor neighborhood, then checked an authoritative IR textbook and official NumPy and scikit-learn semantics before selecting an original semantic merge trace.

implementation.accessibility: The figure uses a native table with a descriptive aria-label, explicit block and item IDs, numeric scores, rank labels, and arrows in text. Borders, ordering, labels, and bold retained sets carry all meaning without color. The established learning-figure, visual-panel, and cm-grid primitives collapse safely within 390 CSS pixels, inherit dark-mode tokens, and switch to a high-contrast light palette for print.
